body.heading: Everyone knows the outside feeling
paragraphs: Standing at the edge of a game. Watching a group laugh. Hoping someone notices. Almost everyone has felt it — which means almost everyone knows exactly how powerful one small sentence can be: 'Do you want to play with us?'
Includers are people who say that sentence. Here is how they do it.

body.heading: Move 1 and 2: notice, invite
paragraphs: Notice. Look up from your game once in a while. Who is alone? Who is watching? Includers have their eyes open.
Invite. Walk over — do not just shout across the playground — and ask: 'We're playing tag. Do you want to join?' A real invitation has a person going to get them.

body.heading: Move 3 and 4: make room, learn the name
paragraphs: Make room. Scoot over on the bench. Deal them in. If teams are picked, pick the new person early — before the end, not as an afterthought.
Learn the name. Ask it, remember it, use it. A name turns 'that kid' into a person, and being called by your name feels like a door opening.

body.heading: If they say no
paragraphs: Sometimes a person says, 'No thanks, I like drawing alone right now.' That is fine! Including is offering the door — not pulling people through it. Smile, say 'Okay, the offer stays open,' and mean it.

body.heading: Think and talk
paragraphs: 1. Remember a time someone included you when you felt outside. What exactly did they do? How long did it take them — ten seconds?
2. Who at your school might be waiting for an invitation this week? What is your plan?

takeaway: Includers notice who is alone, walk over and invite them, make real room, and learn their name — and they respect a 'no thanks' too.
